question: Does an intervention work, when every group will get it in the end?

hemming2018.cite: Hemming et al. (2018). Reporting of stepped wedge cluster randomised trials: extension of the CONSORT 2010 statement with explanation and elaboration. BMJ 363: k1614.
hemming2018.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC6225589) on 20 Nov 2026; the article is online-only (k1614), so places are given as its sections, tables and CONSORT items; in-text reference numbers are left out of the quotes

lazic2010.cite: Lazic (2010). The problem of pseudoreplication in neuroscientific studies: is it affecting your analysis? BMC Neuroscience 11: 5.
lazic2010.checked: the definition of an experimental unit read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC2817684) on 20 Nov 2026; the in-text reference number is left out

steps.title: All start as control
steps.text: Every cluster (a hospital, a school, a region) begins under the usual conditions, and is measured there.

quotes.text: The SW-CRT involves randomisation of clusters to different sequences. These sequences dictate the order (or timing) with which each cluster will switch to the intervention condition.

steps.title: Randomise the order
steps.text: Chance, not readiness or eagerness, decides which clusters switch first and which wait.

quotes.text: A sequence of codes defining the order of implementation of the treatment conditions for each cluster. More than one cluster can be allocated to each sequence.

steps.title: Step across
steps.text: At each planned step another group of clusters switches to the intervention and stays there, until all have it.

quotes.text: A planned point at which a cluster or group of clusters crosses from control to intervention.

steps.title: Measure each period
steps.text: Outcomes are collected in every cluster in every period, before and after its switch.

quotes.text: Each cluster contributes data to the analysis from each measurement period.

steps.title: Adjust for time
steps.text: Intervention periods come later than control periods, so anything that changes over time mixes into the comparison. Compare within periods, and say how time was handled.

quotes.text: Observations collected under the control condition are therefore, on average, from an earlier calendar time than observations collected under the intervention condition.
A SW-CRT which does not adjust for time is analogous to a simple uncontrolled before and after experiment

history-trend.text: Changes external to the trial may create underlying secular trends.

unit-of-analysis.text: An experimental unit is defined as the smallest entity that can be randomly assigned to a different treatment condition

exercise.title: Why time must be adjusted for
exercise.intro: Four groups of clusters, five periods; group 1 switches after period 1, group 4 after period 4. Outcomes drift upward over time whatever happens. Move the trend and compare the two estimates of the effect.

quote.text: Time is a potential confounder because it is associated with both the treatment condition and the outcome.
quote.where: table 2, imbalance of the design with respect to time

exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise.
exercise.model: Each cell's outcome is 50 points, plus the trend times the period number, plus a true effect of 4 points once the group has switched, plus seeded noise (about ±3 points).

limits: The card's defining paper, Hussey & Hughes (2007, Contemporary Clinical Trials), was not read: it is not in Europe PMC's open full text. The quotes come from the CONSORT extension for stepped-wedge trials, Hemming et al. (2018).
The exercise compares only two simple estimates; real analyses fit mixed models with period effects and correlation over time, as Hemming et al. (2018) describe under item 12a.
The card's example (the Gambia Hepatitis Intervention Study) is not quoted: no source on it was read for this page.
